results.title: State of the GPU Rental Market, October 2026 | FastGPU
highlights:
In the week to October 10, NVIDIA's Blackwell GPUs and the H200 were the hardest to rent on demand. The providers that publish stock information had a B300 rentable in 75% of their stock checks, a B200 in 76% and an H200 in 76%, while 15 of the 24 GPUs with enough signal to measure were rentable in every check. Over the same days, the cheapest posted B200 did not move at all: it stood at $3.69/hr in each of the last 7 daily fixings, set by the same provider every day, while the typical provider's price rose. The GPU rental market in October 2026 behaves like two markets: a tight one for Blackwell and H200, priced in a narrow band and getting dearer, and a loose one for older cards that are always in stock, priced far apart and noisy at the floor.

...

Every figure is a snapshot as of October 11, 2026, and every figure is a link. Live prices are as of 4:04 PM UTC that day, availability covers completed UTC days through October 10, and the daily fixings are the ones frozen at 07:00 UTC on October 11. Click any number to reach the page or API row behind it, which shows the current value; where a link and this report disagree, the link is current and the report is dated.

...

- Blackwell and H200 are scarce on demand. In the week to October 10, the B300 was rentable in 75% of stock checks, the B200 in 76%, the H200 in 76%, and the RTX PRO 6000 in 79%, while 15 GPUs were rentable in 100% of checks.
- The H100 SXM had the week's biggest drop. Its rentable share fell from 100% to 87% week on week (it was back at 100% on October 10), and all 8 of its confirmed list-price changes in the last 60 days were rises.
- The floor holds while list prices climb. The price index stands at 99.1, 0.9% below its August base, yet the price-change log holds 81 rises against 4 cuts. The B300's median rose from $8.50 to $9.51 in a week while its floor did not move.
- Rent runs far above the chip's book cost. An H100 SXM rents for a median $3.95/hr; written off over CoreWeave's 6-year schedule, the chip costs $0.48 per GPU-hour and pays for itself in 8.7 months rented around the clock.
- The best GPU per dollar depends on which price you use. At each GPU's floor, the MI355X buys the most benchmarked throughput per rented dollar in one MLPerf® Inference v6.1 scenario, 5,343 tokens/s per $/hr (derived, unverified); at the median price, the B200, B300, GB200 and MI300X are close to a tie.

...

A price is only useful if the GPU is there to rent. The GPU Availability Index records, at every refresh of FastGPU's price feed, each provider's own stock signal for each on-demand and community offer: a stock tier, a yes or no for the exact machine shape, or a live count of rentable hosts. Once a UTC day is complete it is frozen and never revised. The headline share is simple: of the stock checks that carried a signal over the last 7 completed days, the share that found the GPU rentable. In the week to October 10 that came to 27,310 signalled checks across every GPU.

Coverage is the first caveat. Only 5 of the 30 providers in the feed publish stock information today: Hyperstack, QuantaCloud, RunPod, TensorDock and Vast.ai. Offers from everyone else count as listed, never as in stock or sold out, and a share is only stated with at least 12 signalled checks from at least 2 providers, so one provider's stock is never presented as the market's. The index measures the observable slice of the market, which leans toward marketplaces and specialized GPU clouds.

...

## 2. Prices: a flat floor under rising list prices

Two of FastGPU's price series point in opposite directions this autumn. The GPU Cloud Price Index, a Jevons index of the cheapest rentable price for each tracked GPU, stands at 99.1: 0.9% below its base of August 13, with 8 of 18 tracked GPUs cheaper, 7 pricier and 3 flat. By that measure GPU rental prices have gone sideways, as our September report on whether GPU cloud prices are falling found with less data.

The price-change log, which records confirmed moves in providers' own posted rates and leaves out marketplace hosts, tells a different story. Of its 85 entries, 81 are rises and 4 are cuts. In the 60-day window to October 10, every confirmed list-price change for the four flagship data-center GPUs was a rise: 8 for the H100 SXM across 5 providers, with a median step of 14.3%; 6 for the H200 (median step 17.5%); 7 for the B200 ( 17.7%, or $1.20 per GPU-hour); and 6 for the B300 ( 10.4%). One recorded example: RunPod's on-demand B200 went from $6.79 to $7.99 per GPU-hour on October 8. FastGPU's monthly State of GPU prices for September counted 15 posted prices that rose and 0 that fell.

The two series reconcile once you look at who sets the floor, which the daily fixings record each day at 07:00 UTC. For the H100 SXM it was a Vast.ai host on 7 of 7 fixing days, and the same holds for the A100 80GB, L40S and RTX PRO 6000. For the B200 and B300 it was DeepInfra on 7 of 7 days, and for the H200, DeepInfra on 4 of 7. Marketplace hosts reprice constantly and are not list prices; the B200 and B300 floors have not changed once in 67 recorded one-day changes since August 4. Neither kind of seller responds to the list-price rises at the specialized GPU clouds, so the floor, and an index built on floors, stays flat while the price a typical buyer meets climbs.

The medians show that climb directly. Between the fixings of October 5 and October 11, the B300's on-demand median across 10 providers outside the hyperscalers rose from $8.50 to $9.51 per GPU-hour ($9.51 / $8.50 = 1.119, a rise of about 12%), and the B200's from $6.89 to $7.13, while both floors stayed exactly where they were. The H100 SXM median held at $3.95. A week of fixings is a short record and nothing here is a forecast, but the budgeting lesson is plain: a floor that does not move is not evidence that prices are stable. Budget from the median, and check the price-change log for the providers you use.

...

The GPU price volatility and spread page measures how much posted GPU prices move and how far apart providers price the same chip. Volatility is the standard deviation of the one-day log change in each GPU's daily floor over the last 30 days. Spread is the ratio of the 90th to the 10th percentile of each provider's lowest on-demand price, each provider outside the hyperscalers counted once. Read beside who sets the floor and how often list prices change, the two markets from the introduction separate cleanly.

| GPU | Floor volatility, 30 days | Spread, P90 / P10 | Floor set by | List-price changes, 60 days (rises / cuts) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| B200 | 0.0% a day | 1.68x | DeepInfra, 7 of 7 days | 7 / 0 |
| B300 | 0.0% a day | 1.69x | DeepInfra, 7 of 7 days | 6 / 0 |
| H200 | 13.2% a day | 1.81x | DeepInfra, 4 of 7 days | 6 / 0 |
| RTX PRO 6000 | 6.3% a day | 2.00x | Vast.ai, 7 of 7 days | 8 / 1 |
| H100 SXM | 9.6% a day | 2.55x | Vast.ai, 7 of 7 days | 8 / 0 |
| L40S | 13.9% a day | 2.85x | Vast.ai, 7 of 7 days | 5 / 0 |
| A100 80GB | 28.9% a day | 3.53x | Vast.ai, 7 of 7 days | 5 / 1 |

Floor volatility mostly measures who sets the floor. Where a fixed-price seller holds it, as DeepInfra does for the B200 and B300, it is zero. Where a marketplace host holds it, the floor jumps whenever that host's machine is rented or withdrawn. The H100 SXM shows the pattern: its largest one-day move in the window was +35.4%, from $1.32 to $1.79 on September 11; from September 10 to October 5 the floor ran up 41.5% to $1.87, then fell 20.8% to $1.48 by October 7. The record starts on August 4, so each GPU has at most 67 one-day changes: read these figures as a comparison between GPUs with wide error bars, not as a risk model.

Spread runs the other way from scarcity. The GPUs that are hardest to rent are priced in the tightest band: the B200's 90th-percentile provider charges $8.59 and its 10th-percentile provider $5.10, across 12 providers. For the A100 80GB the same ratio is 3.53x ( $3.52 against $1.00 across 15 providers). Provider choice is worth more the older the GPU: on an A100 80GB, moving from the 90th-percentile provider to the 10th cuts the hourly rate by about 72% (1 - $1.00 / $3.52 = 0.72), while on a B200 the binding question is whether anyone has stock. Our map of the cheapest cloud GPUs explains where the low-end offers come from and what they trade away.

Three prices for the same GPU-hour

Floor, on-demand median outside the hyperscalers, and hyperscaler median, daily fixing of Oct 11, 2026

| Gpu | Floor | On-demand median | Hyperscaler median |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A100 80GB | $0.87 | $1.93 | $3.55 |
| H100 SXM | $1.68 | $3.95 | $6.88 |
| H200 | $2.69 | $4.54 | $10.00 |
| B200 | $3.69 | $7.13 | $14.00 |
| B300 | $4.89 | $9.51 | $16.40 |

Source: FastGPU daily fixings, Oct 11, 2026, CC BY 4.0

The basis is the gap between the price a contract follows and the price you pay. It matters now because CME Group's exchange NYMEX has asked the CFTC to approve two cash-settled futures contracts on GPU rental prices, one for the H100 and one for the B200, settling on the monthly average of Silicon Data's H100 rental index and its B200 counterpart - NYMEX Submission No. 26-370. Each contract covers 730 GPU-hours, one GPU for an average month. FastGPU does not reproduce the index values, which belong to their publisher; its own fixings show how far apart the prices a buyer might actually pay sit. In the October 11 fixing, the H100 SXM's on-demand median outside the hyperscalers was $2.27 above the floor and the hyperscaler median another $2.93 above that. For the B200 the two gaps were $3.44 and $6.87. A hyperscaler customer paying $6.88 for an H100 SXM is paying about four times the $1.68 floor ($6.88 / $1.68 = 4.1).

The contracts follow on-demand prices at specialized GPU clouds in the United States, and the filing does not say whether marketplace hosts count. A marketplace renter hedging with such a contract would carry something like the first gap, a hyperscaler customer the second. The GPU futures explainer covers the terms and the review timeline. These are posted prices: not transactions, not a settlement reference and not a forecast.

results.title: GrabGPU vs Silicon Analysts' Cloud GPU Pricing Tracker: Stop Pricing GPUs You Can't Rent — GrabGPU blog
highlights:
Silicon Analysts is a solid reference for big-cloud pricing. Its tracker covers AWS, Azure, GCP, CoreWeave, Lambda, RunPod and Crusoe, with filters for H100 SXM5, H200, B200, B300, TPU v5p, TPU Trillium and MI300X. The pricing matrix has On-Demand, Spot and Cap. Block columns, and a separate table shows spot and reserved discounts by provider. If you’re planning a long hyperscaler contract or a TPU budget, bookmark it.

...

GrabGPU is built for the ML engineer who already knows the price and needs to know whether the card can be rented.

- Stock comes with every price. In the site’s words, “Every row carries the stock the provider reported at our last check”. The in-stock page ranks only capacity confirmed available, cheapest first.
- Data from the providers themselves. Prices come from five public APIs (Shadeform, Vast.ai, RunPod, Lium and QuantaCloud), never from another comparison site. One piece of our code decides what “cheapest” and “in stock” mean. If a source fails, we log it and skip it, so the rest of the site stays up.
- Fresh data. The GrabGPU homepage describes its data as “The same snapshot the pages render, refreshed every hour.”
- On-demand prices up front. Spot prices never headline a page. A spot instance can be taken back mid-run, so it isn’t the same product as an on-demand hour. Leading with spot makes every card look cheaper than you can actually rent it.
- Free JSON, no key./api/best-deals.json and /api/gpus.json give you the snapshot directly, and every offer includes a `rent_url`. There’s also a plain-text `/llms.txt` for AI assistants.

The cheapest rate for a card shifts as providers fill up and free up capacity. We track that from our own snapshots:

Cheapest price per GPU-hour that was listed on at least 2 of the last 3 days (3-day median of the daily low), to 19 Oct 2026. Source: GrabGPU's own snapshots of Shadeform, Vast.ai, RunPod and Lium, the data behind grabgpu.com/gpus/. Chart made 19 Oct 2026.

results.title: Is GPU compute tight? The answer is in contract length | SecondSource
highlights:
## Key takeaways

CoreWeave, a cloud company that specializes in renting out GPUs, the chips AI runs on, says rental prices rose about 25% starting in July. Yet a public index that the website getdeploying compiles from the list prices on dozens of providers' websites read only a 5% rise over a year in mid-September. Both numbers can be right. Almost all of CoreWeave's revenue comes from customers on contracts, while the index collects only the hourly, stop-any-time prices listed on websites (pay-as-you-go), so the two numbers measure different prices. Where compute is visibly tight, with more would-be renters than machines, is contract length: customers who sign for only three to six months pay 2.5 to 4 times the price of a five-to-six-year contract. That is above the gap of about 2 times between renting by the hour and signing for three years in the public market (SecondSource's conversion), but the two multiples cover different terms, so the gap can only be called high. No multiple calculated the same way exists for earlier years, so how much tighter than in past years cannot be said. Long contracts also require 20% to 30% up front. In October, after another provider raised list prices, the index's one-year rise reached 18%. CoreWeave's third-quarter results will show how fast new prices lift the average price across all of CoreWeave's contracts.

...

On the August 11 earnings call, CoreWeave CFO Nitin Agrawal described "our July pricing changes which included an approximately 25% increase across SKUs" (call transcript; also the investor presentation attached to CoreWeave's US$3 billion convertible notes issue on September 17). An SKU is a product model.

In the same period, the getdeploying public index read only a 3.3% rise over four weeks and 5% over a year for the week of September 14. SecondSource's September 18 daily brief drew a conclusion from the gap: the tightness is concentrated in newly signed short-term contracts, out of sight of public prices.

...

CoreWeave's second-quarter 10-Q says 98% of revenue comes from committed contracts and only about 2% from pay-as-you-go. CoreWeave's pricing page lists the H100, one of NVIDIA's GPU models, at US$6.16 per GPU per hour, the figure read on October 18. The site keeps no older versions, so whether this price moved around July can't be checked. In the public index, CoreWeave also appears at US$6.16.

So the 25% most likely went into the prices of new and renewed contracts: even if the listed price did move, the change would touch only about 2% of revenue. The CFO did not say which kind of price the 25% refers to; this reading rests on the 10-Q and the pricing page. The two numbers also cover different periods, so the two cannot be compared directly: the 25% is one company's single price change in July, and the 5% is a year's rise in dozens of providers' listed prices.

...

## Six: In October, another company's listed prices moved

For the week of October 12, getdeploying's reading became 9% over four weeks and 18% over a year; SecondSource's recomputation from getdeploying's public weekly data matches. In the same period Nebius, another GPU rental company, raised listed prices from October 1 (Nebius pricing page). The H100 went from US$3.85 to US$4.50 an hour, and the increases across the H100 and three other NVIDIA GPU models, the H200, B200 and B300, ranged from 17% to 21%.

So the public index can see price increases; what the index sees are increases in listed prices. The index is calculated by GPU model, and in the week of October 12, 21 of 26 models rose; getdeploying hasn't broken out which providers changed prices or how much each contributed.

Back to the September 18 call. Its first half, that tightness is concentrated in newly signed short contracts, is read here as price increases concentrated in new and renewed contracts, with a high short-to-long gap; that half broadly holds, but no one has disclosed how much of new signings short contracts make up. Its second half, that public prices can't see the tightness, narrows to this: the public index can't see increases in contract prices.

...

Details of the public index. Each week getdeploying records every provider's pay-as-you-go listed price. getdeploying takes a median for each provider and then a median across providers, one vote per provider, leaving out reserved and spot prices. SecondSource recomputed October 12 against September 14 from getdeploying's public weekly data: the median change across the 26 models is 8.6%, and against October 13, 2025 it is 18.2%. Nebius's new prices from October 1 were reported by the press by September 17 (Investing.com): the H100 from US$3.85 to US$4.50, the H200 from US$4.50 to US$5.40, the B200 from US$7.15 to US$8.50 and the B300 from US$7.85 to US$9.50. Several outlets called it the second increase in three months. All five data-center models in the index rose between September 14 and October 12: the H100 from US$3.34 to US$3.51, the H200 from US$4.44 to US$4.86, the B200 from US$6.52 to US$7.99, the B300 from US$7.87 to US$8.99 and the A100 from US$1.75 to US$1.82. The rise is uneven across generations: the H100 is up 5% over four weeks, the B200 up 23%. Compute Desk, another index provider, builds its index from completed transactions. Compute Desk says the B300 pay-as-you-go price rose 17 days in a row to a record on October 15, at about US$7 to US$10 an hour, about 64% above November 2025. That account comes from a single secondhand source. The September 18 call also said that a near-double-digit quarterly rise in the public index in the fourth quarter would mean the two measures had converged. A 9% rise over four weeks is already close, but what rose is the listed price itself.

results.title: Neocloud pricing climbs while AI inference costs fall — TechReaderDaily
results.author: M Mireille Otsuka Staff reporting
highlights: The upward leg is not subtle. Nebius raised major GPU prices 17% to 21%, and short-duration capacity negotiations have reached $40 million to $50 million per megawatt, per Seeking Alpha's September analysis. CoreWeave signed new compute capacity contracts at higher prices in the third quarter of 2026, adding $25 billion in commitments. Set those against the Vera Rubin roadmap and you have a three-year contract written at 2026 prices for hardware that will produce tokens at a fraction of 2026 cost. That is a good trade for a seller with a backlog and a bad trade for a buyer who signed without a price-reset clause.

results.title: AI Compute Prices Rise as Investors Weigh Neocloud Debt Risks | TokenPost
results.author: Simon Yoon
highlights: At Tuesday’s auction for computing capacity, per-megawatt prices continued to climb, Marc Boroditsky, Nebius’ chief revenue officer, said. This measure captures the revenue a provider can charge for a set amount of computing capacity. Neoclouds buy Nvidia graphics processing units (GPUs), build data centers and rent that computing power to customers. Providers serve companies that need computing capacity without building all the infrastructure themselves.

results.title: LITEON and QCT Showcase NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 ...
results.author: Irene Chou, Chizuru lizuka
highlights:
- LITEON and QCT jointly showcase an AI infrastructure solution supporting the NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 platform at OCP Global Summit 2026, addressing the growing demands of next-generation high-density AI computing through system-level integration.
- Featuring LITEON's 110kW Power Shelf designed for NVIDIA MGX architecture and rack-level power technologies, the collaboration with QCT helps customers improve AI deployment efficiency, system resilience, and energy efficiency.

LITEON Technology (2301.tw) and Quanta Cloud Technology (QCT), a leading provider of data center and AI solutions, jointly showcased an AI rack-level infrastructure solution supporting the NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 platform at the 2026 OCP Global Summit. The demonstration features LITEON's 110kW Power Shelf integrated within a rack-level power architecture, highlighting how advanced power delivery and system integration can support the growing token-processing requirements driven by agentic AI while improving computing performance and energy efficiency for AI factories.

As AI computing density continues to increase, power infrastructure has become a critical factor in determining overall data center performance. In modern AI racks where GPUs, networking equipment, and thermal management are tightly integrated, power conversion efficiency, dynamic load management, and rack space utilization directly impact deployable compute capacity and operational efficiency. Excessive power system footprint can reduce space available for computing resources, while power conversion losses generate additional heat that increases cooling requirements and operating costs. As a result, next-generation AI infrastructure requires power architectures optimized not only for power density, but also for efficiency, responsiveness, and system resilience at the rack level.

LITEON showcases its 110kW Power Shelf designed to support NVIDIA MGX architecture. Delivering high power density within a compact footprint, the solution provides the rack-level power required by NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 systems while maximizing space available for compute resources. Equipped with high-efficiency power conversion, intelligent load balancing, and digital power management capabilities, the solution is designed to accommodate rapid power fluctuations associated with AI training, inference, and Agentic AI workloads, ensuring reliable operation while reducing energy loss and thermal burden. Combined with QCT's expertise in AI platforms, system design, and data center integration, the two companies are working closely on platform-level co-design and validation to help customers accelerate deployment of high-density AI infrastructure built on the NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 platform.

...

Product lines include hyper-converged and software-defined data center solutions as well as servers, storage, and network switches from 1U to entire racks with a diverse ecosystem of hardware components and software partners to fit a variety of business verticals and workload parameters. www.qct.io
